1023.title: Cornelius and Cyprian (16 September)
1023.hook: a pope and a bishop, friends who disagreed and both died as martyrs
1023.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saints Cornelius and Cyprian together on 16 September, and both names are said in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holy Name of Mary, the last word of Luke's sentence. Your line was Mary. Whose name did you say like it mattered? Day one thousand twenty-three.

A stack of letters, crossing the sea between two cities. One writer is Cornelius, bishop of Rome. The other writer is Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, in North Africa. They are writing in the aftermath of a persecution. Christians had been ordered to sacrifice to the Roman gods, and some gave in to save their lives. Now the pressure has eased, and those same people are at the church door, asking to come back in. What do you do with them? Two bishops had to answer that together, and they didn't always see it the same way. Today, two friends the Church keeps on one day.
screen: `TWO CITIES, A SEA, A STACK OF LETTERS.` → `THOSE WHO GAVE IN.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH THEM?`

segments.voice: The people at the door were called the lapsed: those who had fallen. Some in the Church said never. Once you deny Christ, the Church cannot take you back. A Roman priest named Novatian took that line so hard that he set himself up as a rival bishop of Rome. Others said the opposite: let them all back in, no questions. Cornelius chose a middle way. Welcome them home, after a time of penance. Mercy, but not pretending nothing happened. Now the friendship, which didn't start smoothly. When Cornelius was chosen, Cyprian held back at first, waiting to be sure the choice was sound. Then he backed him firmly, and wrote to him as a brother. On the lapsed, Cyprian had begun stricter, and he worked his way, with other bishops, to a path close to Cornelius's. Friends who disagreed, and kept writing. Cyprian wrote a whole treatise on the unity of the Church, with images like rays from one sun and branches from one tree. Paul's line in the Douay-Rheims could stand over both men: "Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." Then both were taken. Cornelius was sent into exile and died there, and the Church honors him as a martyr. Cyprian was arrested later and tried. The account of his trial says that when the sentence of death was read, he answered with two words: Deo gratias. Thanks be to God. In the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass, the Roman Canon, their names are said side by side: Cornelius, Cyprian. Still together.
screen: `THE LAPSED AT THE DOOR.` · `MERCY, AFTER PENANCE.` · `A FRIENDSHIP THAT STARTED SLOWLY.` · `DEO GRATIAS.` · then, large: `THE UNITY OF THE SPIRIT IN THE BOND OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a letter in your head. Settle, and breathe. These two men kept their friendship going on paper, so choose someone whose views rub against yours, and begin, silently: Dear, and their name. First line: one thing in them you honestly respect. Their courage, their care for someone, their stubborn loyalty. Second line: one place you see it differently, said plainly, without heat. Then stop. No third line about who's right. Let the letter sit there, unsent. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just wish them well. The bell holds the time.

Lapsed, the word for those who had denied the faith under persecution and wanted back in. Cornelius and Cyprian, bishops of Rome and Carthage, disagreed on how to welcome them, and both died for the faith.
Your line: friends who disagreed. Today, say one honest good thing about someone you disagree with, to them or about them, and leave the argument for another day. Day one thousand twenty-three.

1024.title: Joseph of Cupertino (18 September)
1024.hook: a slow student whose prayer was so intense that stories say he floated, patron of exam takers
1024.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memory of Saint Joseph of Cupertino on 18 September, and students ask his prayers before exams; Franciscans honor him as one of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cornelius and Cyprian, a pope and a bishop who kept writing through their disagreements. Your line was friends who disagreed. What good thing did you say about someone? Day one thousand twenty-four.

Who gets turned away by a religious order? Joseph of Cupertino did, the story goes. A poor boy from a small town in southern Italy. Slow at his lessons. Clumsy. So lost in his own head that people teased him for wandering around with his mouth hanging open. He asked the friars to take him, and they sent him away. When he was finally let in, it was to work in the stable. Today, the saint students pray to before a test. Which has a joke folded inside it, because in the stories Joseph is bad at tests.
screen: `TURNED AWAY.` → `TAKEN IN, TO WORK THE STABLE.` → `THE SAINT OF TESTS.`

segments.voice: The stable worker kept praying, and over time the friars saw what was in him and let him study for the priesthood. Study did not go well. Here's the story Catholics tell. At one exam, the examiner opened the Gospel and asked him about a single passage, and it was the one text he knew well. He passed. At the next, the story goes, the first candidates answered so well that the bishop passed the rest of the group without questioning them, and Joseph was in that group. That's why students ask his prayers before exams. Then the strange part. Stories say that when Joseph prayed, especially at Mass, joy would seize him and he would rise off the ground. People came to see. Church authorities questioned him. His superiors, uneasy with the crowds, moved him to quiet friaries, out of sight. Catholics hold the floating stories in different ways. What they honor him for is his humility and his prayer. And underneath it all is a moment in Luke's Gospel. Jesus rejoices and thanks his Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent. The Douay-Rheims finishes the line: "and hast revealed them to little ones." Joseph was a little one in that sense. Not clever, not polished, a little lost. But his prayer was so whole that, in the stories, it lifted him. So he's patron of exams not because he was smart, but because he wasn't, and he was carried through anyway. For Catholics who ask his prayers, a prayer before a test isn't a trick for better grades. It's someone small asking for help, the way Joseph did.
screen: `THE ONE TEXT HE KNEW.` · `STORIES SAY HE FLOATED.` · `HIDDEN FROM THE CLEVER.` · `CARRIED THROUGH.` · then, large: `SHOWN TO LITTLE ONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a student. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is learning something hard right now. A child with homework, a teenager facing finals, a friend studying for a license, someone learning a new language at fifty. Think of the test in front of them, and the nerves. If you pray, you can ask Saint Joseph of Cupertino to pray for them, or pray for them in your own way. If you don't, just hold them in mind and wish them a steady head. The bell holds the time.
Little ones, Jesus's phrase for people like Joseph of Cupertino: the slow, poor student, taken in to work the stable, whose prayer stories say lifted him off the ground. Patron of exams.
Your line: patron of exams. Today, send a word of encouragement to someone facing a test of any kind. Keep it short, and don't ask how they think it'll go. Day one thousand twenty-four.

1025.title: Januarius (19 September)
1025.hook: a bishop-martyr of Naples whose relic of blood is said to liquefy; the Church hasn't ruled on it
1025.tomorrow: Andrew Kim Taegon and companions (20 September)
1025.howItsDone: On 19 September, and on some other days in the year, the reliquary of Saint Januarius is shown in the cathedral of Naples while the faithful pray and wait to see whether the blood liquefies; elsewhere Catholics may keep his optional memorial.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph of Cupertino, the slow student who was carried through. Your line was patron of exams. Who did you encourage before a test? Day one thousand twenty-five.

The cathedral in Naples is packed, and everyone is waiting. Up front, a priest holds a small glass reliquary. Inside is something dark and solid, which the people of Naples say is the dried blood of their patron saint. The priest turns it slowly, again and again, so the crowd can see. People pray, some of them out loud. And they watch to see whether, today, it will turn to liquid. When it does, a cry goes up. When it doesn't, the city worries. Today, the bishop at the center of all that waiting. Januarius.
screen: `A PACKED CATHEDRAL.` → `A SMALL GLASS VESSEL.` → `WILL IT TURN TO LIQUID?`

segments.voice: First, the man. Tradition says Januarius was a bishop of Benevento, in southern Italy, killed for his faith in a Roman persecution, near Naples. Beyond that, little can be confirmed. His relics came to Naples, and Naples took him as its own. He is the city's patron. Second, the blood. Tradition says it was gathered after his death and kept. The vessels are kept in the cathedral, and on his feast and on some other days in the year the reliquary is brought out, and the people wait. Often, witnesses say, the dark mass turns liquid. Sometimes it doesn't. Third, what the Church says, and this matters. The Church hasn't ruled on it. It allows the devotion. It doesn't require anyone to believe that the change is a miracle. People have offered natural explanations, and the question stays open. Catholics are free to hold it either way. So the center of this day isn't a verdict. It's a city standing together, hoping. A line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims, is close to the heart of it: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." Whatever happens inside that glass, the people of Naples have kept a martyr's death close, and treated it as precious. And there's something else in the scene. The waiting itself. A crowd that has nothing to do but pray and watch and wait together. Some days the answer comes quickly. Some days it's slow. Some days it doesn't come at all, and they come back anyway.
screen: `A BISHOP AND MARTYR.` · `THE BLOOD IN THE GLASS.` · `THE CHURCH HASN'T RULED.` · `A CITY WAITING TOGETHER.` · then, large: `PRECIOUS IN THE SIGHT OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait with Naples. Settle, and breathe. Don't reach for anything. Let the sit be a stretch of waiting, the way the crowd waits in front of the glass. Notice what you're waiting on in your own life: news, a change, an answer that hasn't come. Hold it loosely. Then widen the circle to the people of Naples, and to anyone in your own town who is waiting today, by a hospital bed, by a phone, at a door. If you pray, you can pray for Naples, and ask Saint Januarius to pray for it. If you don't, simply wait alongside them, without needing an answer. The bell holds the time.
Januarius. The bishop and martyr, patron of Naples, whose blood in a glass vessel is said to turn liquid. The Church hasn't ruled on it.
Your line: the people wait. Today, when you have to wait, in a line, on hold, for news, let the waiting be a kind of prayer, or at least a kind of patience. Day one thousand twenty-five.

1026.title: Andrew Kim Taegon and companions (20 September)
1026.hook: Korea's first native priest and 102 companions
1026.howItsDone: On 20 September Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Andrew Kim Taegon, priest, Paul Chong Hasang, and companions, martyrs; Korean Catholic communities keep it as a great day of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Januarius, and a city waiting in its cathedral. Your line was the people wait. What did you have to wait for, and how did you wait? Day one thousand twenty-six.

A few books, carried home from China. That's where the Catholic story in Korea begins, as Korean Catholics tell it. Not with missionaries stepping off a ship, but with Korean scholars reading Christian books, arguing over them, and wanting more. One of them traveled to Beijing, was baptized there, and came home and baptized his friends. A Church, started by its own people, reading their way in, before any priest had come to them. Then the faith was forbidden, and the hunting began. Today, its martyrs: a priest, a layman, and their companions.
screen: `A FEW BOOKS FROM CHINA.` → `SCHOLARS WHO BAPTIZED EACH OTHER.` → `THEN THE FAITH WAS FORBIDDEN.`

segments.voice: Start with Andrew Kim Taegon. He grew up in a Catholic family when being Catholic in Korea could cost your life, and it cost his father's. As a young man he was sent abroad to study for the priesthood, and he was ordained a priest far from home. Then came his choice. He could have stayed where it was safe. Instead he slipped back into Korea in secret, to say Mass, hear confessions, and find a way to bring more priests in. He served only a short time before he was caught. He was tortured, tried, and beheaded near Seoul, still a young man. Tradition keeps a farewell letter he wrote to his people, urging them to hold together in love and not be shaken. Next, Paul Chong Hasang. A layman, not a priest. His father, too, had died for the faith. He spent his life trying to bring priests to Korea, and he wrote a defense of the faith addressed to the government. He was killed as well. And then the companions. Men and women. Nobles and servants. Catechists, mothers, young people. The Church keeps them together on one day, priest and layman, noble and servant. Jesus says in the Douay-Rheims: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone. But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Some Korean Catholics read their own story in that verse. A Church begun by laypeople reading books, and planted in the ground by martyrs. Which is why the line for today names the whole country.
screen: `A PRIEST WHO WENT HOME IN SECRET.` · `A LAYMAN WHO WROTE IN DEFENSE.` · `NOBLES AND SERVANTS, ONE CHURCH.` · `THE GRAIN OF WHEAT.` · then, large: `IT BRINGETH FORTH MUCH FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a grain of wheat for Korea. Settle, and breathe. Rest one open hand in your lap, as if a single grain of wheat lay in it. Small, dry, easy to lose. Let it stand for the people of Korea, north and south: its families, its churches, the people there who believe and the people who don't, the families divided by the border. With each out-breath, let the grain go into the ground, a wish for good to grow there. Hold anyone, anywhere, who can't practice their faith in the open. If you pray, you can pray for Korea, and ask Saint Andrew Kim and his companions to pray for it. If you don't, simply wish its people peace. The bell holds the time.
Kim Taegon, baptized Andrew: the Korean priest who went home in secret to serve his people, with the layman Paul Chong Hasang and the men and women who died with them.
Your line: korea's martyrs. Today, learn one thing about a Korean neighbor's story, a church, a family, a meal, or simply say a prayer or a good wish for Korea. Day one thousand twenty-six.

1027.title: Matthew (21 September)
1027.hook: a tax collector at his table hears two words and gets up
1027.howItsDone: The feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, is kept on 21 September with its own Mass readings, often including the call at the tax booth from Matthew 9.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Andrew Kim Taegon and his companions. Your line was korea's martyrs. Did you hold Korea in mind for a moment? Day one thousand twenty-seven.

A table by the road, coins stacked on it, a ledger open. The man behind it collects taxes, and in the gospels his trade is named in the same breath as sinners. Nobody stops to chat. Then someone does stop. He looks at the man at the table and says two words. Follow me. The gospel doesn't record a speech, a debate, a night to think it over. It records a man standing up. Today, Matthew.
screen: `A TABLE BY THE ROAD.` → `TWO WORDS: FOLLOW ME.` → `A MAN STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: The whole call takes one verse. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus sees a man sitting in the custom house, named Matthew, and says to him: "Follow me. And he arose up and followed him." That's it. Mark and Luke tell the same scene and call the man Levi; Catholic tradition reads Levi and Matthew as one person. Now look at what he left. Some readers point to a difference: a fisherman like Peter could go back to his boats, and in John's gospel he does. A man who walked away from a tax post, those readers say, had no boat to go back to. And what does he do first? Luke says he made Jesus a great feast in his own house. Matthew's gospel says Jesus sat at table in the house, and many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him. Some onlookers asked his disciples why their teacher ate with such people. Jesus answered with a doctor's logic: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill." Then he sent them to a line from the prophet Hosea: "I will have mercy and not sacrifice." So the first thing a newly called man did was invite his old crowd to meet the one who called him. He didn't hide where he came from. The book that opens the New Testament carries his name, and Catholic tradition holds him to be its author. In that gospel, the man is named plainly: Matthew the publican. He kept the old label right next to the new life.
screen: `ONE VERSE: FOLLOW ME, AND HE AROSE.` · `SOME SAY: NO BOAT TO GO BACK TO.` · `HIS FIRST ACT: A DINNER FOR HIS CROWD.` · `HE KEPT THE NAME: MATTHEW THE PUBLICAN.` · then, large: `I WILL HAVE MERCY AND NOT SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one thing to follow. Sit back and let your breathing slow. Notice what's on your table right now, the thing you keep checking, the stack you keep counting. It might be your phone, a worry, a grudge. Choose one, and for these two minutes, set it down. Literally, if you can: turn the phone over, close the tab. If you pray, you can hear the two words, follow me, and simply stay with them. If you don't, notice what it feels like to stand up from something. The bell holds the time.
Matthew. The tax collector who heard two words, got up from his table, and then threw a dinner so his old friends could meet the man who called him.
Your line: he arose and followed. Today, when you catch yourself stuck at the same table, stand up once, on purpose, and go toward something better. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

1028.title: Cosmas and Damian (26 September)
1028.hook: two doctors, remembered for healing without a fee, whose names are said at Mass
1028.howItsDone: Saints Cosmas and Damian are remembered on 26 September, and their names are said in the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I) whenever a priest uses it with its full list of saints; some Catholic doctors and hospitals keep their feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matthew, who left his tax table for good. Your line was he arose and followed. What did you stand up from? Day one thousand twenty-eight.

Before you see a doctor these days, there's usually a form. Insurance, payment, a signature at the bottom. Now strike all of that. A clinic with no front desk and no bill. You walk in sick, you're treated, you walk out, and nobody asks for anything. That's the story the Church tells about two brothers who practiced medicine long ago. Their names are still spoken in a prayer of the Mass. Today, Cosmas and Damian.
screen: `A CLINIC WITH NO BILL.` → `TWO BROTHERS, BOTH DOCTORS.` → `NAMES SPOKEN AT MASS.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as tradition tells it. Cosmas and Damian were brothers, twins in some tellings, who trained as physicians somewhere in the eastern part of the Roman world. They were Christians, and they treated the sick without taking payment. The Eastern churches gave them a title for it, a Greek word that means, roughly, the ones without silver. During a persecution, the story goes, they were arrested and put to death for their faith. Historians can say very little for certain about their lives; what is sure is that the Church kept their names. Why did they work for free? Their story points straight to a line Jesus gave the apostles when he sent them out to heal. In the Douay-Rheims: "Freely have you received, freely give." Healing, in that line, isn't a product. It's a gift passed along. Now the surprising part. If you go to a Catholic Mass where the priest uses the first Eucharistic Prayer, the old Roman Canon, listen for a list of names. Mary, Joseph, the apostles, then a run of early popes and martyrs, the same list that names Cornelius and Cyprian. At the end of that list come two doctors: Cosmas and Damian. When the priest prays that list in full, as the Missal allows him to shorten it, these brothers are named in the middle of the Mass. Some doctors and pharmacists claim them as patrons, and some hospitals carry their names. Their feast puts two ideas side by side: that a healer's skill is a gift, and that people who care for the sick are worth remembering by name.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS WHO HEALED WITHOUT PAY.` · `THE ONES WITHOUT SILVER.` · `FREELY HAVE YOU RECEIVED, FREELY GIVE.` · `NAMED IN THE ROMAN CANON.` · then, large: `FREELY GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a doctor. Settle in and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has cared for your body: a doctor, a nurse, a pharmacist, a parent who sat up with you through a fever. Remember one specific moment of their care. If you pray, you can name them before God, the way the Mass names Cosmas and Damian. If you don't, just hold them in mind with gratitude. And when the bell rings, think about whether you could actually tell them. The bell holds the time.
Without silver, the old title for healers like Cosmas and Damian, brothers and doctors who, tradition says, healed without charging, and whose names are still spoken in the Roman Canon.
Your line: the free doctors. Today, notice the people who look after other people's bodies: the nurse, the pharmacist, the parent up at night. Learn one of their names. Day one thousand twenty-eight.

1029.title: Wenceslaus (28 September)
1029.hook: the good king of the carol was a duke, and his own brother had him killed
1029.howItsDone: Saint Wenceslaus is remembered on 28 September, a national feast in the Czech Republic; Catholics there keep it with Mass, and his statue in Prague's Wenceslas Square is a gathering place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cosmas and Damian, the brothers who healed without a bill. Your line was the free doctors. What did you give away without charging? Day one thousand twenty-nine.

Snow, deep and crisp and even. A king looks out his window on the feast of Stephen, sees a poor man gathering firewood, and sets off through the storm with food and wine, his page stepping in his footprints to keep from freezing. That's the Christmas carol. It's an English Victorian song, written long after the man it names. The real Wenceslaus was not a king, and his story doesn't end at a warm table. It ends at a church door. Today, Wenceslaus.

segments.voice: Wenceslaus, Václav in Czech, was a duke of Bohemia, in the lands that are now the Czech Republic. Tradition remembers him as a ruler who prayed, helped the poor, and tried to govern as a Christian when the court around him was split over the faith. His grandmother Ludmila, also honored as a saint, raised him in it. Not everyone in the family was pleased. His younger brother, Boleslaus, wanted power. The old accounts tell it this way: Boleslaus invited Wenceslaus to a feast. The next morning, as Wenceslaus walked to Mass, his brother and his men attacked him at the door of the church, and he died there. Brother against brother, at the doorway to worship. It's a story as old as Genesis. In Genesis, after Cain kills Abel, God asks him where his brother is, and Cain answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Am I my brother's keeper?" In the Wenceslaus story, that old question comes back at a church door. In time, people began to honor Wenceslaus as a martyr, and he became the patron of the Czech people. In Prague, a great square bears his name, with his statue on horseback at the top. The carol calls him a king anyway: good king Wenceslas. Not a title he held. In the song, a title he earned.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a divided family. Let your shoulders drop and breathe. Bring to mind a family that's split, yours or someone else's: siblings who don't speak, parents and children who can't be in the same room. Don't fix it. Just hold both sides, without choosing a winner. If you pray, you can name them before God, and ask for one small thaw. If you don't, simply wish them, each of them, a little peace. The bell holds the time.
Wenceslaus. A duke of Bohemia who governed as a Christian, was killed by his brother's men at a church door, and is remembered in a carol as the good king.
Your line: good king. Today, do what the king in the carol does: bring something warm to someone out in the cold. A meal, a coat, a ride, a visit. Day one thousand twenty-nine.
